title: Death Certificate 2026: 21-Day Rule, CRS Apply & Delays
meta_description: Register a death within 21 days free on crsorgi.gov.in. Delayed routes explained, plus the 2026 rule sending cases beyond two years to a judicial magistrate.

hero.one_liner: Register the death within 21 days and the certificate is free and quick. Miss that window and the process hardens at every stage, so this guide covers both routes

sections.title: 📌 The 21-Day Rule Decides Everything That Follows
sections.content:
Under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, a death must be reported to the Registrar within 21 days. Inside that window registration is free and the certificate usually arrives in 2 to 5 days.

After 21 days the process hardens in stages: a late fee up to 30 days, District Registrar permission up to one year, an executive magistrate's order between one and two years, and a judicial magistrate's order beyond that. If a death has just happened, this is the one deadline worth protecting.

sections.heading: What the Certificate Records and Why Everything Needs It
content: A death certificate is the government's official record that a person has died, issued by the local registrar under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act. It carries the name, age, date, time and place of death, the medical cause, and the registration number.

Nothing downstream moves without it. Bank accounts stay frozen, insurance claims sit unprocessed, property cannot transfer, pension cannot start, and a surviving spouse cannot claim widow or widower benefits.
The document families actually need is not the hospital's notification slip. That slip is only the input; the registrar's certificate is the legal proof.
Because so many institutions demand an original, treat copies as a planning decision rather than an afterthought. Most families underestimate how many they will be asked for.

One practical note before you start: the registrar records the informant's name permanently on the entry. Whoever registers should be someone the family can reach later if a correction is ever needed.

sections.heading: 🗓️ The Registration Windows and What Each Requires

items.desc: Report to the registrar of the area where the death occurred. The certificate is typically issued in 2 to 5 days.
The registrar still handles it directly, with a small state-set late fee. The process is otherwise unchanged.
Needs permission from the prescribed authority with supporting documents. The 2023 amendment allows self-attested documents in place of affidavits.
An order from a District Magistrate, SDM, or authorised Executive Magistrate after verification. Plan for weeks, not days.
The 2026 amendment moves this tier to the judiciary, making it a court process rather than a counter application.

sections.title: 🆕 Law Changed in 2026: Deaths Older Than Two Years Now Go to a Judicial Magistrate
sections.content:
Parliament passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026 in early August, after the Lok Sabha cleared it on 31 July. It splits delayed registration into two tiers instead of one.

A delay of one to two years still goes to a District Magistrate, SDM, or authorised Executive Magistrate. A delay beyond two years now needs an order from a Judicial Magistrate First Class under the new Section 13(3A).

Amendments like this commence from a date the government notifies, so ask your registrar which tier applies before filing. If your delay is nearing two years, filing sooner keeps you in the simpler executive route.

sections.heading: Who Can Register the Death
content: The law places the duty on the household: the head of the family, whoever was in charge of the deceased, a relative, or any person present at the time of death can register it.
For a hospital death, the institution's records officer prepares the death notification and reports the event. The family still completes the registration and collects the certificate.
For a death at home, the doctor or medical attendant who was present certifies the cause. Where no doctor attended, the registrar records it as an uncertified death based on family testimony.
You do not need to be the next of kin to register. You do need identity proof and a stated relationship, because the registrar records who the informant was.

If nobody in the family registers the death, the law still expects the event to be reported by whoever was responsible for the deceased at that time. Hospitals and institutions carry their own reporting duty separately from yours.

sections.heading: Registering Within 21 Days: The Normal Route

steps.title: Collect the death notification
steps.desc: Hospitals issue it from the death registration cell, usually the same day. For a home death, get the medical attendant's certificate from the attending doctor.

steps.title: Go to the right registrar
steps.desc: Registration happens where the death occurred, not where the deceased lived. A death in a Delhi hospital is registered in Delhi even if the family lives in Patna.

steps.title: Fill the death registration form
steps.desc: This is separate from the hospital slip. It asks for full name, age, address, occupation, date, time, place and cause of death, plus the informant's details.

steps.title: Submit with documents
steps.desc: Attach the notification or medical certificate, the deceased's ID, the informant's ID, and address proof. Registration inside 21 days is free in most bodies.

steps.title: Collect multiple copies
steps.desc: The certificate is usually ready in 2 to 5 days. Ask for several certified copies at this point rather than returning later for each one.

sections.heading: 📋 Documents by Situation
rows: Issued by the hospital's registration cell on doctor's certification
From the doctor or nurse who attended the deceased
Registration proceeds only after these are complete
Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport or ration card
Identity proof of the person registering the death
Utility bill, ration card, or rental agreement
The 2023 amendment permits self-attested documents; some offices still ask for a notarised affidavit

sections.heading: When You Have Missed the 21 Days
content: Between 21 and 30 days, the registrar still handles it. You pay a small late fee set by the state and the process otherwise runs normally.

Between 30 days and one year, you need written permission from the District Registrar or the prescribed authority, along with supporting documents. The 2023 amendment allows self-attested documents in place of affidavits, though many state offices still ask for a notarised affidavit in practice.

Between one and two years, registration happens only on an order from a District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, or an Executive Magistrate authorised by the District Magistrate, after verification that the death occurred.
Beyond two years, the 2026 amendment routes the case to a Judicial Magistrate First Class. That is a court order rather than an administrative one, so budget for legal help and a longer wait.
There is no outer time limit. Deaths from decades ago can still be registered, but you will need strong corroborating evidence rather than just an application form.
The stages count from the date of death, not from when you first tried. Starting the paperwork inside a stage still counts even if the office takes longer to finish it.

Whatever the stage, arrive with your evidence assembled rather than assembling it after a rejection. Delayed applications that are complete on first submission move noticeably faster than ones sent back for missing papers.

sections.heading: Applying Online Through the CRS Portal

steps.title: Check your state on crsorgi.gov.in
steps.desc: The Civil Registration System is the national platform, but coverage and features differ by state. Some states route you to their own municipal portal.

steps.title: Register an account
steps.desc: Sign up with email and mobile, verify the OTP, and log in. Keep those credentials since status tracking runs through the same account.

steps.title: Fill the form and upload
steps.desc: Enter the deceased's details and the death particulars, then upload the notification, ID proofs and address proof as clear scans within the size limits.

steps.title: Track the application
steps.desc: Status moves from submitted to under verification to approved. Check every few days because offices often request extra documents through the portal.

steps.title: Download the certificate
steps.desc: Approved certificates can be downloaded as a digital copy, and many states also push them to DigiLocker. Physical collection stays available.

sections.heading: What Goes Wrong at the Counter
content: Incomplete hospital notifications are the most common rejection. A missing time of death, cause, or doctor's signature sends the application back, so check every field before leaving the hospital.
Address mismatches cause quiet delays. If municipal records show one spelling and your documents show another, the file goes to manual verification and can sit for over a week.
Registering at the wrong office wastes the most time. The jurisdiction is where the death happened, and staff cannot transfer an application to another municipal body.

Vague cause-of-death entries create insurance trouble later. Where the hospital writes something general, ask for the most specific medically accurate wording, because insurers query broad causes and some policies exclude specific ones.
For online applications, blurry scans are rejected outright. Scan at reasonable resolution, capture both sides of ID documents, and keep files within the portal's size limit.
Finally, hold on to the acknowledgement or application number. Tracking anything without it, online or at the counter, turns into a fresh search through records.

sections.title: Certified copies to collect upfront
sections.desc: Bank closure, insurance, property transfer, pension, employer records and mutation each want an original. Collecting them together costs a nominal fee per copy and saves repeat visits.

sections.heading: Where You Will Be Asked for It
qualify: Closing bank accounts and releasing balances to nominees
Life insurance and accident claim settlement
Family pension, widow or widower pension, and gratuity
Employer settlement, PF and gratuity claims
disqualify: The hospital's death notification slip alone will not do for any of these
Photocopies without the registrar's seal are refused by most banks
Claims cannot proceed while the death remains unregistered
A certificate with a wrong cause of death can stall an insurance claim until corrected

sections.heading: Special Cases: Hospital, Unnatural, Custody and Abroad
content: Hospital deaths are the simplest. The registration cell prepares the notification with exact time and medical cause, and collecting it before leaving the hospital saves days later.

Unnatural deaths, including accidents and suicides, require an FIR and post-mortem first. Registration proceeds only after police clearance, so the timeline extends well beyond 21 days through no fault of the family.
Deaths in custody or in jail follow a separate track: the administration reports the death and a magisterial inquiry is conducted before registration.

For a death abroad, the Indian mission in that country issues the documentation and the death is recorded under Indian rules on repatriation. Start with the embassy or consulate rather than the local registrar back home.
Where no doctor attended a home death, registration still happens as an uncertified death recorded on family testimony, with the cause left medically unconfirmed.
In each of these situations the registrar still records the death in the normal register once clearances arrive. The certificate that comes out looks the same as any other.

sections.heading: Before the Certificate Arrives: What You Can Start Now
content: Waiting families lose weeks assuming nothing can move until the certificate is in hand. That is not quite true, and a few calls made early shorten everything downstream.

Inform the bank, insurer and employer about the death straight away. Insurers open a claim file on intimation, and banks flag the account so no further debits go through while the paperwork catches up.
Ask each institution for its exact requirement list at the same time. Some want a succession certificate or legal heir certificate alongside the death certificate, and those take weeks of their own.
Gather the deceased's document set in one folder: ID proofs, bank passbooks, policy documents, property papers and the PAN. Every claim afterwards draws from this same pile.

One caution: do not operate the deceased's bank account with an ATM card or existing access after death. Nominee settlement is the correct route, and withdrawals afterwards create legal complications for the family.

sections.heading: After the Certificate: The Settlement Checklist

items.title: Banks and lockers
items.sub: Submit the certificate with nominee ID to release balances and access lockers.

items.title: Insurance claims
items.sub: File with the insurer promptly; most policies expect intimation within a defined window.

items.title: Property mutation
items.sub: Apply at the tehsil with the certificate and succession or legal heir document.

items.title: Pension and PF
items.sub: Family pension, EPF and gratuity all begin with this certificate at the employer or department.

items.title: Records cleanup
items.sub: Remove the name from the ration card and voter roll to prevent verification problems later.

items.title: Subscriptions and utilities
items.sub: Close or transfer electricity, gas, phone and DTH connections in the deceased name.

sections.heading: Death Certificate vs Legal Heir vs Succession Certificate
content: Families often assume the death certificate transfers assets, but it does no such thing. It proves the death occurred, and nothing more.

A legal heir certificate, issued by the tehsildar or revenue authority, records who the surviving heirs are. It is what employers, pension offices and many banks ask for alongside the death certificate.

A succession certificate comes from a civil court and is needed for debts and securities where a nominee is absent or disputed. It costs more and takes months, so it is used when the simpler route will not do.

The practical order is death certificate first, legal heir certificate next, and a succession certificate only where an institution or a dispute demands it. Starting the second step while the first is processing saves real time.

sections.heading: Correcting a Mistake on the Certificate
content: Errors in name spelling, date, age or cause of death are corrected through a written correction application at the issuing registrar, with documentary proof of the correct fact.
Cause-of-death corrections need supporting medical documents from the hospital or attending doctor. Insurers care about this field, so fix it before filing a claim rather than after a query.
Corrections are nominal in cost and usually take a few days. What takes longer is realising the error late, after banks or insurers have already rejected paperwork.
Read the certificate carefully at collection. Checking it at the counter takes a minute and avoids a return trip.
Keep the original and the corrected certificate together afterwards. Institutions occasionally ask why a reissued copy differs from one they already hold on file.

sections.heading: Why the Process Feels Different Across States
content: The Act is central but registration is run by states and local bodies, which is why fees, forms and portals differ. Some states register deaths fully online while others still want a counter visit for the final collection.
Municipal corporations in large cities usually issue faster than rural panchayat registrars, mostly because of volume and staffing rather than rules.
Late fees are set by the state, so the amounts quoted in any guide are ranges rather than fixed figures. Ask the registrar for the current fee rather than assuming.
What does not change across states is the 21-day window and the escalating tiers, because those come from the central Act.
If your state is not on the CRS portal, that is not a problem with your case. Check the state's own municipal portal, since many run parallel systems that feed the same central register.

sections.heading: Official Sources & References
sections.content:
Source: Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969 with the 2023 and 2026 amendments, and the Civil Registration System at crsorgi.gov.in. State municipal bodies set their own fees and processing times.

Because the 2026 amendment commences on a notified date, confirm the applicable tier with your registrar before filing a delayed registration.

sections.text: Twenty-one days is the whole game. Everything after that is paperwork proving what a single form would have recorded for free.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get a death certificate?
faqs.answer:
Registered within 21 days, most registrars issue it in 2 to 5 days. Online applications through the CRS portal move on a similar timeline once documents are verified.

Delayed registration takes longer at every stage, from 1 to 3 weeks for District Registrar permission up to several weeks or months where a magistrate's order is needed.

faqs.question: What happens if a death is not registered within 21 days?
faqs.answer:
Registration is still possible, it just gets harder. Between 21 and 30 days a small late fee applies, and between 30 days and a year you need the District Registrar's written permission with supporting documents.

Beyond a year it needs a magistrate's order. There is no upper time limit, so an old death can still be registered with enough evidence.

faqs.question: What changed in the 2026 death registration law?
faqs.answer:
The Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026 splits delayed registration into two tiers. A delay of one to two years goes to a District Magistrate, SDM or authorised Executive Magistrate, while a delay beyond two years now needs a Judicial Magistrate First Class.

Parliament passed it in early August 2026 after the Lok Sabha cleared it on 31 July. Since such amendments commence from a notified date, confirm with your registrar which tier applies before filing.

faqs.question: Can a death from many years ago still be registered?
faqs.answer:
Yes, there is no outer limit. But under the 2026 amendment a delay beyond two years needs an order from a Judicial Magistrate First Class rather than a district officer, so treat it as a court matter.

Gather corroborating evidence first: cremation or burial records, hospital papers if any survive, an obituary, ration card or voter roll deletion records, and affidavits from witnesses.

faqs.question: Mrityu praman patra kaise banwaye?
faqs.answer:
Maut ke 21 din ke andar us area ke registrar office me jayen jahan death hui thi, aur hospital ka death notification ya doctor ka medical certificate, mrityu vyakti ka ID, apna ID aur address proof jama karein. Is window me registration free hai aur certificate 2 se 5 din me mil jata hai.

Online ke liye crsorgi.gov.in par account banakar apply kar sakte hain, agar aapka state us portal par hai. Ek saath 5 se 10 certified copy le lein, kyunki bank, insurance aur property ke liye alag alag original mangi jati hai.

faqs.question: Where do I register the death, at home or where it happened?
faqs.answer:
Where the death occurred, not where the deceased lived. A death in a Delhi hospital is registered with the Delhi civic body even if the family lives elsewhere.

This trips up families who travel home before registering. Registrars cannot transfer an application to another municipal body, so going to the wrong office costs a full trip.

faqs.question: How many copies of the death certificate should I get?
faqs.answer:
Collect 5 to 10 certified copies at the time of registration. Banks, insurers, property mutation, pension offices and employers each want an original and most do not return them.

Extra copies cost a nominal fee per copy when ordered together, while returning later means a fresh application and another wait.

faqs.question: Is the digital death certificate from the CRS portal valid?
faqs.answer:
Yes. Certificates issued through the Civil Registration System carry legal validity, and many states also deliver them to DigiLocker.

Some offices and older institutions still ask for a physically sealed copy, so keep both a downloaded PDF and certified paper copies.

faqs.question: Can the cause of death be corrected later?
faqs.answer:
Yes, through a correction application at the issuing registrar with supporting medical documents from the hospital or attending doctor.

Do it before filing an insurance claim. Insurers query vague or inconsistent causes, and some policies exclude specific conditions, so the wording on this field matters.

faqs.question: Can a death certificate be issued before the post-mortem is done?
faqs.answer:
No. Where a post-mortem is required, as in accidents and other unnatural deaths, registration waits for the post-mortem report and police clearance.

The delay is procedural and not counted against the family, but it does push the case past the 21-day window in practice.

faqs.question: What if the deceased had no Aadhaar?
faqs.answer:
Aadhaar is not mandatory. Any other government identity document works, including PAN, voter ID, passport or ration card.

Where no document exists at all, the registrar can proceed on family testimony with supporting declarations. Ask the office what it accepts before travelling there.

faqs.question: Is a death certificate needed for an insurance claim?
faqs.answer:
Yes, and it is the first document insurers ask for. The hospital's notification slip is not accepted in its place.

Intimate the insurer about the death immediately even while the certificate is pending, since most policies expect prompt intimation and the claim file can be opened before the certificate arrives.
